---
title: "Joins & Concatenation"
subtitle: "≈ two-table verbs · `join_by()` · `bind_rows()` / `bind_cols()`"
jupyter: python3
---

dplyr has a verb per join type; Polars has one method, `join()`, with `how=`
choosing the type, plus `join_where()` for inequality joins and
`join_asof()` for closest-match joins. Binding rows and columns is one
function, `pl.concat(how=...)`. The one-line translations are in the
[cheatsheet](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-joins). This chapter
covers the defaults behind them. Several differ from dplyr: the join type,
null keys, which key columns survive, row order, and dtype checks.

## In tidyverse {#sec-join-tidyverse}

```r
library(dplyr)
library(nycflights13)

planes |> count(tailnum) |> filter(n > 1)              # is tailnum a primary key?
flights2 <- flights |> select(year, time_hour, origin, dest, tailnum, carrier)
flights2 |> left_join(airlines)                         # natural join: by = "carrier"
flights2 |> left_join(planes, join_by(tailnum))         # year.x, year.y
flights2 |> left_join(airports, join_by(dest == faa))
flights2 |> left_join(weather, join_by(origin, time_hour), relationship = "many-to-one")
flights2 |> anti_join(planes, join_by(tailnum)) |> distinct(tailnum)
employees |> inner_join(parties, join_by(between(birthday, start, end)))
employees |> left_join(parties, join_by(closest(birthday >= party)))
bind_rows(list(a = df1, b = df2), .id = "source")
```

Without being asked, dplyr joins on every shared column when `by` is missing,
keeps the row order of `x`, matches `NA` to `NA`, warns about many-to-many
matches, suffixes clashing columns on both sides (`.x`, `.y`), and merges the
two key columns in `full_join()`. Polars does none of these by default. Each
one is a parameter of `join()`.

## Mental model {#sec-join-model}

```text
 x.join(y, on="k", how=...)                 x = left frame, y = right frame

   x                  y
   k   x-cols         k   y-cols            a match = equal keys
   ──────────         ──────────            null ≠ null (unless nulls_equal=True)
   1   x1  ──────────► 1   y1
   2   x2  ──────┬───► 2   y2a              a key repeated in y repeats its x row
                 └───► 2   y2b              (m:m; checked only with validate=)
   3   x3              4   y4

   how="inner"  matched rows only                             ← the DEFAULT
   how="left"   every x row; y-cols null when unmatched
   how="right"  every y row; x-cols null when unmatched
   how="full"   every row of both; k and k_right unless coalesce=True
   how="semi"   x rows with a match      ┐ filtering joins: x-cols only,
   how="anti"   x rows without a match   ┘ never duplicate a row
   how="cross"  every x row × every y row, no key
```

The other two join methods change only the match rule. `join_where()`
replaces "equal keys" with any Boolean predicate, and `join_asof()` replaces
it with "the closest key", giving at most one match per left row.

## Mechanics {#sec-join-mechanics}

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
import datetime as dt

import polars as pl
from pl_notes import datasets

flights_df = datasets.flights()
airlines_df = datasets.airlines()
airports_df = datasets.airports()
planes_df = datasets.planes()
weather_df = datasets.weather()
```

### Keys {#sec-join-keys}

A primary key must be unique and never null. Check both before you rely on it:

```{python}
planes_df.select(
    n=pl.len(), n_unique=pl.col("tailnum").n_unique(), n_null=pl.col("tailnum").null_count()
)
```

For a compound key, wrap the columns in a struct so that the duplicate check
looks at the combination (≈ `count(time_hour, origin) |> filter(n > 1)`):

```{python}
weather_df.filter(pl.struct("origin", "time_hour").is_duplicated()).height
```

`weather` also has the clock parts `year, month, day, hour`. They look like an
equivalent key, but they are not:

```{python}
weather_df.group_by("origin", "year", "month", "day", "hour").len().filter(
    pl.col("len") > 1
).sort("origin")
```

On 2013-11-03 New York set its clocks back, so 01:00 happened twice. The
time-zone-aware `time_hour` keeps the two hours apart (`01:00 EDT`, then
`01:00 EST`); the clock parts can't. Use the instant as the key (see
[Dates, Times & Durations](../types/datetime.qmd)).

`flights` is keyed by `(time_hour, carrier, flight)`, which has no duplicates.
Where no natural key exists, `with_row_index("id")` adds a surrogate key
(≈ `mutate(id = row_number())`, but 0-based and `UInt32`). Note that
`is_duplicated()` flags **every** copy, where R's `duplicated()` flags only the
later ones.

### Mutating joins {#sec-join-mutating}

Start from R4DS's narrow `flights2`:

```{python}
flights2_df = flights_df.select("year", "time_hour", "origin", "dest", "tailnum", "carrier")

flights2_df.join(airlines_df, on="carrier", how="left", maintain_order="left").head(3)
```

`maintain_order="left"` keeps the row order of `flights2_df`
(@sec-join-order). Polars has no natural join, so `on` is required:

```{python}
#| error: true
flights2_df.join(airlines_df, how="left")
```

**Clashing columns.** `flights2` and `planes` both have `year` (the year of
the flight vs the year the plane was built). Polars renames only the **right**
copy, using `suffix=` (default `"_right"`). dplyr would give `year.x` and
`year.y`. To rename the left copy too, rename it before the join:

```{python}
flights2_df.join(
    planes_df.select("tailnum", "year", "type"), on="tailnum", how="left",
    suffix="_built", maintain_order="left",
).head(3)
```

**Different key names.** `left_on="dest", right_on="faa"` ≈
`join_by(dest == faa)`. The output keeps `dest` and drops `faa`.
`coalesce=False` keeps both (≈ `keep = TRUE`).

**Compound keys.** Pass a list. `time_hour` is `Datetime("us",
"America/New_York")` in both tables, and it has to be: the unit and the zone
must match (@sec-join-dtypes):

```{python}
flights_weather_df = flights2_df.join(
    weather_df.select("origin", "time_hour", "temp", "wind_speed"),
    on=["origin", "time_hour"], how="left", maintain_order="left",
)
flights_weather_df.head(3)
```

### `how=` and `coalesce=` {#sec-join-how}

R4DS's toy tables show every join type. Each entry is the result's
`(rows, columns)`:

```{python}
x_df = pl.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2, 3], "x": ["x1", "x2", "x3"]})
y_df = pl.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2, 4], "y": ["y1", "y2", "y4"]})

hows = ["inner", "left", "right", "full", "semi", "anti"]
joined = {how: x_df.join(y_df, on="k", how=how) for how in hows}
{how: (res.height, res.columns) for how, res in joined.items()}
```

If you leave out `how=`, you get `inner`, and unmatched rows disappear with no
message. `right` moves `k` into the right frame's position (`x, k, y`).
`full` returns **two** key columns, and `k` is null for the row that only
exists in `y`:

```{python}
x_df.join(y_df, on="k", how="full", maintain_order="left_right")
```

```{python}
x_df.join(y_df, on="k", how="full", coalesce=True, maintain_order="left_right")
```

| `how` | `coalesce=None` (default) | Key columns in the output |
|---|---|---|
| `inner`, `left` | coalesce | one, with the left name (`dest`) |
| `right` | coalesce | one, with the **right** name (`faa`); dplyr keeps `dest` |
| `full` | **don't** coalesce | `k` + `k_right` (or `dest` + `faa`) |
| `semi`, `anti` | — | left columns only |
| any, with an expression key | **never** coalesce | every key twice (@sec-join-expr-keys) |

: Which key columns survive {.striped}

`how="cross"` takes no key: passing `on=` raises `ValueError`.

### Duplicate keys and `validate=` {#sec-join-validate}

A key that repeats on both sides multiplies rows. If you forget `time_hour`
when joining weather, three flights turn into 26,115 rows, one for every hour
recorded at their airports:

```{python}
flights_df.head(3).join(weather_df, on="origin").height
```

dplyr warns about an unexpected many-to-many relationship. Polars says
nothing, because the default is `validate="m:m"`, which checks nothing. State
the relationship you expect:

```{python}
#| error: true
flights_df.head(3).join(weather_df, on="origin", validate="m:1")
```

`"m:1"` requires unique keys on the right, `"1:m"` on the left, and `"1:1"`
on both. The docstring says the streaming engine doesn't support `validate`,
but in 2.0.0 a lazy `validate="1:1"` join of `flights` to `planes` still
raised under the default `collect()`. dplyr's `unmatched = "error"` has no
parameter equivalent; check with an anti join (@sec-join-filtering).

### Nulls and NaN in keys {#sec-join-nulls}

```{python}
x_null_df = pl.DataFrame({"k": [1, None, 3], "x": ["x1", "x_null", "x3"]})
y_null_df = pl.DataFrame({"k": [1, None, None], "y": ["y1", "y_null_a", "y_null_b"]})

x_null_df.join(y_null_df, on="k", how="left", maintain_order="left")
```

The null key matched nothing. dplyr's default (`na_matches = "na"`) would
have matched it twice. Pass `nulls_equal=True` to get that behaviour:

```{python}
x_null_df.join(y_null_df, on="k", how="left", nulls_equal=True, maintain_order="left_right")
```

`NaN` is different: it **does** match `NaN`, with no flag:

```{python}
nan_df = pl.DataFrame({"k": [1.0, float("nan")], "v": [1, 2]})
nan_df.join(nan_df, on="k", maintain_order="left")
```

So the 2,512 flights with a null `tailnum` can never match a plane. More on
null semantics in [Missing Values](../types/missing.qmd).

### Key dtypes {#sec-join-dtypes}

Integer keys of different widths join without complaint. Any other mismatch
is a `SchemaError`, including different time zones:

```{python}
#| error: true
flights2_df.join(
    weather_df.with_columns(pl.col("time_hour").dt.convert_time_zone("UTC")),
    on=["origin", "time_hour"],
)
```

| Left key | Right key | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `Int64` | `Int32`, `UInt32` | joins; a left join keeps the left dtype |
| `Int64` | `Float64` or `String` | `SchemaError` |
| `String` | `Categorical` | `SchemaError` |
| `Datetime("us", "America/New_York")` | `Datetime("us", "UTC")`, `Datetime("us")`, `Datetime("ms", …)` | `SchemaError` |

: Key dtype pairs (verified on Polars 2.0.0) {.striped}

In R, a POSIXct's `tzone` attribute only changes how it is displayed. In
Polars, the zone is part of the dtype (see [Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd)),
so align keys with `cast()` or `dt.convert_time_zone()` before you join.

### Row order: `maintain_order=` {#sec-join-order}

The default, `maintain_order="none"`, promises no order. The docstring warns
that it "might differ across Polars versions or even between different
runs". Eager left joins often happen to keep the left order, which makes the
default easy to trust by accident. An eager inner join doesn't:

```{python}
{
    order: airlines_df.join(flights2_df, on="carrier", maintain_order=order)["carrier"]
    .head(4).to_list()
    for order in ["none", "left_right"]
}
```

`airlines` starts with `9E`, but the default result follows `flights`. Lazy
queries run on the streaming engine by default in 2.0, and there even a left
join loses the left order:

```{python}
def left_join_lazily(**kwargs) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return (
        flights_df.with_row_index("row").lazy()
        .join(airlines_df.lazy(), on="carrier", how="left", **kwargs)
        .collect()
    )

{order: left_join_lazily(maintain_order=order)["row"].is_sorted() for order in ["none", "left"]}
```

The other options are `"right"`, and `"left_right"` / `"right_left"` (order by
the first frame, then by the second). `"left"` matches dplyr. Keeping an order
costs speed, so skip it if you `.sort()` the result anyway.

### Filtering joins {#sec-join-filtering}

`semi` and `anti` keep only the left columns, and they return each left row
at most once, however many matches it has. Of the 1,458 airports, 3 are
origins and 101 are destinations:

```{python}
{
    key: airports_df.join(flights_df, left_on="faa", right_on=key, how="semi").height
    for key in ["origin", "dest"]
}
```

An anti join finds **implicit missing** keys: values a foreign key points to
that are absent from the target table. These four destinations aren't in
`airports`, so a left join leaves their airport names null:

```{python}
flights_df.join(airports_df, left_on="dest", right_on="faa", how="anti").select(
    pl.col("dest").unique().sort()
)
```

### Non-equi joins: `join_where()` {#sec-join-where}

R4DS's party example: there is one party per quarter, and each employee goes
to the party for the quarter that contains their birthday:

```{python}
def dates(*isos: str) -> pl.Series:
    return pl.Series(isos).str.to_date()

parties_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "q": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "party": dates("2022-01-10", "2022-04-04", "2022-07-11", "2022-10-03"),
    "start": dates("2022-01-01", "2022-04-04", "2022-07-11", "2022-10-03"),
    "end": dates("2022-04-03", "2022-07-11", "2022-10-02", "2022-12-31"),
})
employees_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Ana", "Bo", "Cy", "Di", "Ed"],
    "birthday": dates("2022-01-05", "2022-02-14", "2022-07-11", "2022-09-30", "2022-12-25"),
})

employees_df.join_where(
    parties_df, pl.col("birthday").is_between(pl.col("start"), pl.col("end"))
).sort("name", "q")
```

Cy matches two quarters because of a data-entry bug: Q2 ends on the day Q3
starts. `join_where()` takes any number of predicates and combines them with
AND. A name that exists in only one frame refers to that frame. A name that
exists in both refers to the **left** column; write the right one with its
suffix. `pl.col("q") < pl.col("q")` raises no error: it compares the left `q`
with itself and returns no rows. A self-join on `overlaps` finds the bug:

```{python}
parties_df.join_where(
    parties_df,
    pl.col("start") <= pl.col("end_right"),   # overlaps(start, end, start, end)
    pl.col("end") >= pl.col("start_right"),
    pl.col("q") < pl.col("q_right"),          # each pair once, no self-pairs
).select("q", "start", "end", "q_right", "start_right", "end_right")
```

| dplyr `join_by()` helper | `join_where()` predicate(s) |
|---|---|
| `x > y`, `x <= y`, … | `pl.col("x") > pl.col("y")` |
| `between(x, lo, hi)` | `pl.col("x").is_between(pl.col("lo"), pl.col("hi"))`, both ends inclusive |
| `within(x_lo, x_hi, y_lo, y_hi)` | `pl.col("x_lo") >= pl.col("y_lo"), pl.col("x_hi") <= pl.col("y_hi")` |
| `overlaps(x_lo, x_hi, y_lo, y_hi)` | `pl.col("x_lo") <= pl.col("y_hi"), pl.col("x_hi") >= pl.col("y_lo")` |
| `cross_join()` + `filter()` | any Boolean expression, including `|` and arithmetic |

: Inequality helpers {.striped}

`join_where()` is marked experimental. It accepts `how="inner"` (default),
`"left"`, or `"right"`. Its docstring says row order is not preserved, so sort
the result.

### Rolling joins: `join_asof()` {#sec-join-asof}

`join_asof()` works like a left join, except that each left row takes the one
right row whose key is **closest**. With the default `strategy="backward"`,
that is the last right key `<=` the left key, the same as R4DS's
`closest(birthday >= party)` (the latest party on or before each birthday):

```{python}
employees_df.join_asof(
    parties_df.select("q", "party"), left_on="birthday", right_on="party"
)
```

No party comes on or before Ana's birthday, so she gets null. Unlike `join()`,
`join_asof()` keeps the right key column (`party`).

| dplyr | `join_asof()` |
|---|---|
| `closest(x >= y)` | `strategy="backward"` (default) |
| `closest(x > y)` | `strategy="backward", allow_exact_matches=False` |
| `closest(x <= y)` | `strategy="forward"` |
| — | `strategy="nearest"` (either direction) |
| equality on other columns first | `by="g"` (or `by_left` / `by_right`) |
| — | `tolerance="30d"`: no match beyond this distance |

: `closest()` and its options {.striped}

**Both frames must be sorted by the key.** Without `by`, Polars checks this
and raises an error:

```{python}
#| error: true
employees_df.sort("birthday", descending=True).join_asof(
    parties_df, left_on="birthday", right_on="party"
)
```

With `by`, each group must be sorted, and Polars **cannot check** that. It
emits a `UserWarning` on every call, even when the data is sorted, and
unsorted data silently gives wrong matches:

```{python}
trades_df = pl.DataFrame({"sym": ["A", "B", "A", "B"], "t": [1, 5, 7, 9]})
quotes_df = pl.DataFrame({"sym": ["A", "A", "B", "B"], "t": [6, 0, 8, 2], "px": [11, 10, 21, 20]})

trades_df.join_asof(quotes_df, on="t", by="sym")   # quotes not sorted by t
```

All four matches are wrong. Sort the data yourself, then pass
`check_sortedness=False`, which also silences the warning:

```{python}
trades_df.join_asof(quotes_df.sort("t"), on="t", by="sym", check_sortedness=False)
```

### Concatenation {#sec-join-concat}

| `pl.concat(how=)` | Columns matched by | Dtype mismatch | ≈ dplyr |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"vertical"` (default) | position; names must be identical | error | `bind_rows()` of identical frames |
| `"vertical_relaxed"` | position; names must be identical | cast to supertype | — |
| `"diagonal"` | name; missing → null | error | `bind_rows()` |
| `"diagonal_relaxed"` | name; missing → null | cast to supertype | `bind_rows()` (closest) |
| `"horizontal"` | — (equal heights required) | — | `bind_cols()` |
| `"horizontal_extend"` | — (shorter frames padded with null) | — | — |
| `"align"` (= `"align_full"`), `"align_inner"`, `"align_left"`, `"align_right"` | shared columns, used as a sorted key | — | `reduce(dfs, full_join)` |

: Concatenation strategies in 2.0 {.striped}

`bind_rows()` matches columns by **name**. The default `"vertical"` requires
the same names in the same order:

```{python}
#| error: true
ewr_df = airports_df.filter(pl.col("faa") == "EWR").select("faa", "name")
jfk_df = airports_df.filter(pl.col("faa") == "JFK").select("name", "faa")
pl.concat([ewr_df, jfk_df])
```

```{python}
pl.concat([ewr_df, jfk_df], how="diagonal")
```

The `_relaxed` variants cast to the supertype, and the supertype of `Int64`
and `String` is `String`. Numbers become text where `bind_rows()` would raise
an error. In 2.0, `"horizontal"` requires equal heights (its `strict=`
parameter is deprecated as redundant). To pad shorter frames with nulls, use
`"horizontal_extend"`:

```{python}
#| error: true
pl.concat([x_df, pl.DataFrame({"z": [True]})], how="horizontal")
```

`pl.union()` is **not** dplyr's `union()`. It is `pl.concat()` without a
row-order guarantee, and it keeps duplicates (`UNION ALL`, not `UNION`).

### Set operations {#sec-join-setops}

dplyr's `union()`, `intersect()` and `setdiff()` compare whole rows, treat
`NA` as equal, and drop duplicates. In Polars, build them from
`concat` + `unique` and from semi/anti joins on every column. The joins need
`nulls_equal=True`:

```{python}
a_df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, None], "y": ["a", "b", "c"]})
b_df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [2, None, 4], "y": ["b", "c", "d"]})
every_col = {"on": a_df.columns, "nulls_equal": True}

{
    "intersect, nulls unequal": a_df.join(b_df, on=a_df.columns, how="semi").rows(),
    "intersect": a_df.join(b_df, how="semi", **every_col).unique(maintain_order=True).rows(),
    "setdiff": a_df.join(b_df, how="anti", **every_col).unique(maintain_order=True).rows(),
    "union": pl.concat([a_df, b_df]).unique(maintain_order=True).rows(),
}
```

## Where it bites {#sec-join-gotchas}

| dplyr behaviour | Polars behaviour |
|---|---|
| the join type is in the verb's name | `join()` defaults to `how="inner"` |
| no `by` → natural join | `on` is required |
| `NA` matches `NA` | null never matches; `NaN` matches `NaN` |
| `.x` and `.y` on both sides | only the right side gets a suffix (`_right`) |
| `full_join()` merges keys | `k` + `k_right` unless `coalesce=True` |
| output follows `x` | any order unless `maintain_order=` |
| warns on many-to-many | silent unless `validate=` |
| keys of compatible types combine | only integer widths are cast; other mismatches raise |
| `bind_rows()` matches by name | `"vertical"` needs identical names in identical order |

: The differences at a glance {.striped}

### An expression key turns off coalescing for every key {#sec-join-expr-keys}

`left_on` / `right_on` accept expressions, so you can join daily
precipitation by the calendar date of `time_hour`. But once **any** key is an
expression, Polars coalesces none of them, so even the plain `origin` comes
out twice:

```{python}
weather_daily_df = weather_df.group_by("origin", date=pl.col("time_hour").dt.date()).agg(
    precip_day=pl.col("precip").sum()
)

flights2_df.select("origin", "time_hour").join(
    weather_daily_df, left_on=["origin", pl.col("time_hour").dt.date()],
    right_on=["origin", "date"], how="left", maintain_order="left",
).head(2)
```

`coalesce=True` doesn't change this, and an `.alias()` inside a key raises
`'alias' is not allowed in a join key, use 'with_columns' first`. Taking that
advice and building the key as a column makes every key plain:

```{python}
flights2_df.select("origin", "time_hour").with_columns(
    date=pl.col("time_hour").dt.date()
).join(weather_daily_df, on=["origin", "date"], how="left", maintain_order="left").head(2)
```

### A null after a left join is not the same as no match

```{python}
{
    "temp is null": flights_weather_df["temp"].null_count(),
    "no weather row": flights2_df.join(weather_df, on=["origin", "time_hour"], how="anti").height,
}
```

The 17 extra nulls come from weather rows that exist but have no `temp`
value. To count unmatched rows, use an anti join, or test a right-side column
that is never null.

## Recipes {#sec-join-recipes}

**Add airline and destination names to flights.** Validate each lookup and
keep the flight order:

```{python}
flights_df.select("time_hour", "carrier", "flight", "dest").join(
    airlines_df.rename({"name": "airline"}),
    on="carrier", how="left", validate="m:1", maintain_order="left",
).join(
    airports_df.select("faa", dest_name="name"),
    left_on="dest", right_on="faa", how="left", validate="m:1", maintain_order="left",
).head(3)
```

**Weather at departure, with gaps.** The exact join on `(origin, time_hour)`
misses 1,556 flights. 932 of them are scheduled after `weather` ends
(2013-12-30 18:00), and the rest fall in hours with no observation. A backward
as-of join takes the latest observation within 3 hours:

```{python}
flights2_df.sort("time_hour").join_asof(
    weather_df.select("origin", "temp", obs_time="time_hour").sort("obs_time"),
    left_on="time_hour", right_on="obs_time",
    by="origin", tolerance="3h", check_sortedness=False,
).select(no_obs=pl.col("obs_time").null_count())
```

That leaves 794 flights without an observation, 790 of which are more than
3 hours past the end of the record.

**Which tail numbers are missing from `planes`?** This is R4DS's question.
There are 722 distinct missing values, null included, since null never
matches. Two carriers account for most of the flights:

```{python}
flights_df.join(planes_df, on="tailnum", how="anti").group_by("carrier").agg(
    n_flights=pl.len(), n_tailnums=pl.col("tailnum").n_unique()
).sort("n_flights", descending=True).head(3)
```

**The rate in effect on each date.** A rate table lists the date each value
*starts*, and every date takes the latest start on or before it. Here is a
made-up surcharge per carrier:

```{python}
surcharge_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "carrier": ["AA", "AA", "UA", "UA", "UA"],
    "effective": dates("2013-01-01", "2013-07-01", "2013-01-01", "2013-03-15", "2013-09-01"),
    "surcharge": [25, 40, 30, 35, 45],
})

flights_df.filter(pl.col("carrier").is_in(["AA", "UA"])).group_by(
    "carrier", date=pl.col("time_hour").dt.date()
).agg(n_flights=pl.len()).sort("date").join_asof(
    surcharge_df.sort("effective"), left_on="date", right_on="effective",
    by="carrier", check_sortedness=False,
).filter(
    pl.col("date").is_between(dt.date(2013, 3, 14), dt.date(2013, 3, 15))
).sort("carrier", "date")
```

The UA rate changes on 2013-03-15 and AA's does not.
